article_title: First Impressions: Creating Newsflashes with Impact
citation: Joanne Pfleiderer. (2013). First Impressions: Creating Newsflashes with Impact. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Effective dissemination requires getting the right message to the right people at the right time in the right form
description: The guide's core principle is that dissemination must be matched to audience and medium: "Today, effective dissemination depends on getting the right message to the right people at the right time in the right form." To break through the clutter of competing communications, researchers are advised to assemble the elements the guide enumerates rather than relying on a single channel.
requirements: Researchers need the right elements: a compelling story, engaging visuals, and a set of electronic tools, including email, video, and social media
target_learning_goals: effective communication of research findings to intended audiences
examples: The guide contrasts past practice—posting a report on the web or sending out a press release—with the current need to combine story, visuals, and electronic tools in one communication.
key_sources: Joanne Pfleiderer. (2013). First Impressions: Creating Newsflashes with Impact. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/first-impressions-creating-newsflashes-with-impact

article_title: The Impact of Rhode Island's Charter School Performance Review System
citation: Margaret E. Raymond, PhD; Marzena Sasnal, PhD. (2025). The Impact of Rhode Island's Charter School Performance Review System on the Education Landscape. Center for Research on Education Outcomes, Stanford University. https://credo.stanford.edu
title: Rhode Island's new performance framework sets rigorous, multidimensional quality standards across academic achievement, governance, financial stability, and mission alignment
description: The article describes an enumerated set of quality standards that the new performance framework imposes on existing charter schools. Schools must "demonstrate strong academic gains, measured through standardized assessments" and match or exceed sending district performance; governing boards are accountable for oversight and culture; schools must show long-term financial viability; and they are evaluated on mission fulfillment and service to diverse populations including English learners and students with disabilities. The framework applies these standards from the initial application through renewal, with annual dashboards supporting continuous improvement.
requirements: Applicants must meet very rigorous criteria to be authorized to open a new charter in Rhode Island
Schools receive ongoing performance indicators and annual dashboards so expectations are understood
constraints: Some charter school leaders argued that using the SAT to evaluate career and technical education schools is not an adequate measure of success
target_learners: Rhode Island charter school students, including English learners and students with disabilities
examples: RIDE developed the updated framework after a year of research with charter school practitioners, collecting feedback from parents, community members, advocacy groups, and school leaders
key_sources: Margaret E. Raymond, PhD; Marzena Sasnal, PhD. (2025). The Impact of Rhode Island's Charter School Performance Review System on the Education Landscape. Center for Research on Education Outcomes, Stanford University. https://credo.stanford.edu/reports/item/rhode-island-2025/

article_title: Tough As Nails and Drawing on Kinship: Rigorous and inclusive educational research in Kentucky Appalachia
citation: Emi Iwatani. (2023). Tough as Nails & Drawing on Kinship: Rigorous and inclusive educational research in Kentucky Appalachia [Invited speaker session]. American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, Chicago, IL. https://bit.ly/TANrefs
title: Apply rigor in inclusive research by taking community preconditions seriously when identifying interventions worth studying
description: The presentation proposes a definition of rigor for community-engaged research that treats inclusion as exactness rather than softness. It argues research that helps people work toward futures requires inclusion, and that "rigor (strictness, exactness, rigidity) in our research is applied in taking these preconditions seriously (when identifying the interventions worth studying), and in the studying." This reframes methodological strictness as inseparable from who defines the problems studied.
requirements: Research problem selection must be governed by the community's own preconditions (visibility of futures, inclusion, agency)
constraints: Articulated for partnership-based design research in a specific regional context
examples: The RPP identifies interventions worth studying only after establishing the civic imagination preconditions with district partners
key_sources: Emi Iwatani. (2023). Tough as Nails & Drawing on Kinship: Rigorous and inclusive educational research in Kentucky Appalachia [Invited speaker session]. American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, Chicago, IL. https://bit.ly/TANrefs

article_title: Design Principles for Schools: Putting the Science of Learning and Development into Action
citation: Learning Policy Institute & Turnaround for Children. (2021). Design principles for schools: Putting the science of learning and development into action. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/
title: Engage students in rich, authentic, collaborative learning with scaffolding and Universal Design for Learning
description: The report recommends meaningful and challenging work within and across core disciplines, including the arts, music, and physical education, that builds on students' culture, prior knowledge, and experience. It states that "Students learn best when they are engaged in authentic activities and are collaboratively working and learning with peers to deepen their understanding and to transfer knowledge and skills to new contexts and problems". Recommended supports include inquiry and problem-based learning, performance assessments focused on higher-order thinking, careful scaffolding creating zones of proximal development, and cognitive supports such as Universal Design for Learning that reduce unnecessary cognitive load and use multiple modalities.
requirements: Teachers need opportunities and tools to come to know students' experiences and thinking well, and flexibility to accommodate distinctive pathways to learning
constraints: The report notes learning happens in fits and starts, requiring flexible scaffolding and differentiated strategies to reach common goals
examples: The report recommends tools such as learning surveys, student reflections, observation protocols, formative assessments, and exit tickets for learning about students' experiences and readiness
key_sources: Learning Policy Institute & Turnaround for Children. (2021). Design principles for schools: Putting the science of learning and development into action. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/

article_title: Design Principles for Teacher Preparation: Enacting the Science of Learning and Development
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Hyler, M. E., & Wojcikiewicz, S. (with Rushing, J.). (2025). Design principles for teacher preparation: Enacting the science of learning and development. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/115.854
title: Immerse teacher candidates in rich, experiential learning opportunities with performance-based assessment
description: The report states that all learners, including prospective teachers, actively construct knowledge based on their experiences, relationships, and social contexts, so EPPs should immerse teacher candidates in active and compelling learning opportunities paired with authentic and performance-based assessments. Programs should coordinate coursework and fieldwork to provide a full range of adult learning experiences, including practice, feedback, skill development, and growth in adaptive expertise. Pedagogical activities should promote inquiry and cycles of reflection through complex practice situations.
requirements: Coordination of coursework and fieldwork across the scope and sequence
Authentic and performance-based assessments
target_learning_goals: Analyzing student learning in relation to instruction
Planning curriculum around learning goals and trajectories
examples: Candidates should use a repertoire of teaching strategies that build understanding by enabling discussion, application, practice, feedback, and opportunities to revise
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L., Hyler, M. E., & Wojcikiewicz, S. (with Rushing, J.). (2025). Design principles for teacher preparation: Enacting the science of learning and development. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/115.854

article_title: How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. https://EdTrust.org
title: Students need equitable access to rigorous, culturally sustaining curricula and advanced coursework to thrive
description: The brief argues students "should have access to rigorous, deeper learning and culturally sustaining curricula," because when students see themselves in the work and feel challenged, their belief in reaching their goals strengthens. It recommends guidance and funding for standards-aligned, culturally sustaining curricula and equitable, even automatic, enrollment in advanced coursework.
requirements: Guidance and a review process for selecting curricula aligned to learning standards and culturally sustaining criteria
State education agency staff to support districts with implementation
target_learners: P-12 students, including those inequitably enrolled in advanced coursework
target_learning_goals: Rigorous learning, cultural relevance, and equitable access to advanced coursework
examples: Texas provides guidance for selecting standards-aligned curricula, funding to expand advanced coursework enrollment, and publicly reports advanced coursework data disaggregated by student demographics
key_sources: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628037

article_title: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. (2023). The Education Trust. https://EdTrust.org
title: Students need access to rigorous, culturally sustaining curricula with equitable advanced-coursework enrollment
description: The brief argues that students must be challenged and encouraged to meet high expectations through rigorous, deeper learning and culturally sustaining curricula. It reasons that "When students can both see themselves in the work and feel their teachers challenging them to excel, what follows is a stauncher belief in themselves to reach their goals." Washington's bright spots include state goals calling on districts to equitably enroll students in advanced coursework, guidance for adopting culturally sustaining curricula and standards-aligned curricula, automatic enrollment in advanced coursework in high school, and public reporting of dual credit completion disaggregated by demographics.
requirements: State education agency staff to support curricular needs, guidance on selecting culturally sustaining curricula aligned to learning standards, and a review process for determining whether curricula meet these criteria
constraints: Washington's goals do not explicitly state curricula should be rigorous and culturally sustaining, and lack specific actions for equitable advanced-coursework enrollment or disaggregated enrollment and success data by course type
target_learners: P-12 students, with attention to equitable access for underserved students
target_learning_goals: Rigorous, deeper learning; self-belief in reaching goals; access to advanced coursework and college and career preparation
examples: Washington requires automatic enrollment in advanced coursework in high school and publicly reports dual credit completion disaggregated by student demographics
key_sources: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. (2023). The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED630072

article_title: Making AI-Generated Feedback Matter: From Provision to Student Enactment
citation: Omar Alsaiari, Nilufar Baghaei, Jason M. Lodge, Naomi Winstone, Dragan Gašević, Hassan Khosravi. (2026). Making AI-Generated Feedback Matter: A Large-Scale Study of Feedback Workflows and Student Enactment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11625
title: RiPPLE adaptive peer-learning platform
description: RiPPLE (Recommendation in Personalised Peer-Learning Environments) is the platform in which the study was conducted. As printed, "RiPPLE (Recommendation in Personalised Peer-Learning Environments) is an adaptive learning platform that engages students in creating, evaluating, revising, and practising with peer-generated learning resources." It structures activity across creation, review, and practice stages; peer moderation ratings are aggregated into a submitted-work quality score on a 0-5 scale. Its instrumentation captured fine-grained interaction logs recording every state transition between drafting, reviewing feedback, AI-supported dialogue, revision, and submission, enabling all outcome measures in the study.
requirements: peer moderation against a structured rubric covering accuracy, clarity, alignment with the stated topic, and pedagogical value
fine-grained interaction logging of workflow state transitions
constraints: The underlying language model used for AI-mediated support differed across implementation periods, reflecting the model versions available at each deployment
examples: Across all three conditions, students in each round created one original learning resource, moderated three peer-created resources, and practised ten resources authored by other students
key_sources: Omar Alsaiari, Nilufar Baghaei, Jason M. Lodge, Naomi Winstone, Dragan Gašević, Hassan Khosravi. (2026). Making AI-Generated Feedback Matter: A Large-Scale Study of Feedback Workflows and Student Enactment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11625

article_title: A Taxonomy of LLM-Supported Tasks for Critical AI Literacy in Journalism
citation: Laurence Dierickx, Fredrik Bjerknes, Andreas L. Opdahl, Carl-Gustav Lindén. (2026). A Taxonomy of LLM-Supported Tasks for Critical AI Literacy in Journalism. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00690-0
title: Risk-and-mitigation task tables: each LLM-supported task pairs a baseline prompt with task-specific risks and mitigation strategies
description: The taxonomy is instantiated as four tables (Tables 2-5), one per workflow stage, where each task row gives a definition, a model-agnostic baseline prompt, and a risk-and-mitigation column. The paper says the prompts and risk categories are designed to be transferable across tools and versions, and that "each task in the taxonomy is situated within a risk-based ethical framework and articulated through a baseline prompt." For example, summarisation carries the risk of missing key elements or introducing inaccuracies, mitigated by human reading of the document and cross-checking consistency using multiple models.
requirements: Prompts are intentionally simple and model-agnostic so students can translate journalistic intentions into explicit instructions; recurring tasks such as generation recur across stages but with different risks per editorial object
constraints: The paper notes risks do not disappear but manifest differently depending on how a task is defined
examples: Table 5 pairs personalisation ('Summarise today's news for a reader interested in [topic].') with echo chambers and filter bubbles as risks and ensuring diversity of perspectives as mitigation
key_sources: Laurence Dierickx, Fredrik Bjerknes, Andreas L. Opdahl, Carl-Gustav Lindén. (2026). A Taxonomy of LLM-Supported Tasks for Critical AI Literacy in Journalism. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00690-0

article_title: A Risk-Adaptive and Evidence-Constrained Framework for Generative AI Feedback in Programming Education
citation: Shihao Wang. (2026). A Risk-Adaptive and Evidence-Constrained Framework for Generative AI Feedback in Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29874
title: Risk-adaptive, evidence-constrained framework linking prediction, capacity-aware decision, and grounded feedback generation
description: The article introduces a five-stage framework connecting observation, prediction, decision, generation, and evaluation for personalized programming feedback. Calibrated risk guides intervention timing under fixed feedback capacity, bounded task and code evidence grounds diagnostic statements, and an "Evidence-Gated Progressive Assistance" policy orders support from self-checks through concept reminders to localized hints and focused review. The framework keeps predictive validity, policy value, and feedback quality as distinct evaluation endpoints while using the same temporally ordered evidence.
requirements: Time-valid learner representations with predictors restricted to information available at the intervention point
Student-disjoint evaluation partitions and validation-fitted probability calibration before threshold deployment
constraints: Evaluated retrospectively on recorded trajectories from one introductory programming course; prospective learner outcomes such as knowledge mastery and retention are named as future evaluation targets, not measured here
target_learners: introductory programming students in higher education
examples: The study instantiated the framework with 2993 failed-submission states from 215 students, four matched feedback conditions for 136 cases, and fixed-capacity and sequential threshold policies replayed over recorded trajectories.
key_sources: Shihao Wang. (2026). A Risk-Adaptive and Evidence-Constrained Framework for Generative AI Feedback in Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29874

article_title: Student Development Agent: Risk-free Simulation for Evaluating AIED Innovations
citation: Jianxiao Jiang, Yu Zhang. (2025). Student Development Agent: Risk-free Simulation for Evaluating AIED Innovations. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09183
title: Use LLM-based student development simulation as a risk-free pre-deployment evaluation of AIED innovations to avoid exposing real students to uncertain effects
description: The article argues that because educational interventions may carry irreversible effects, novel AIED designs should be prospectively evaluated before exposure to students. Its framework enables "a risk-free simulation process" that "directly avoids exposing actual students to uncertain effects of new teaching approaches, assessment methods, or adaptive feedback mechanisms," so that initial prototyping and experimentation occur without risking learners' academic or psychological well-being.
requirements: A validated student development agent whose predictions align with real outcomes sufficiently to inform decisions
constraints: The framework is presented as an initial, preliminary evaluation safeguarding students while supporting innovation pace, not a replacement for empirical studies
target_learners: students who would otherwise be exposed to untested AIED interventions
target_learning_goals: anticipating benefits and harms of educational designs on cognitive and non-cognitive development before deployment
examples: The MAIC case study evaluated simulated students' non-cognitive development without administering the course to new real students
key_sources: Jianxiao Jiang, Yu Zhang. (2025). Student Development Agent: Risk-free Simulation for Evaluating AIED Innovations. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09183

article_title: AI refusal in higher education: the right to refuse, the duty to understand and the diagnostic value of non-use
citation: Zagami, J. (2026). AI refusal in higher education: the right to refuse, the duty to understand and the diagnostic value of non-use. Higher Education Research & Development, 45(7), 2287-2294. https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2026.2694409
title: Protect the right to private refusal while holding role-based non-use accountable through a duty to understand
description: The article distinguishes private refusal — a protected right not to use AI in personal intellectual, creative or everyday life — from role-based refusal, which requires justification where AI materially shapes educational, scholarly, administrative or governance activity. The duty to understand 'should not be converted into a managerial requirement to use commercial systems'; it includes the capacity to reject, restrict, audit and critique AI. Refusal is thus one of the most important forms of AI literacy.
requirements: Universities must provide trustworthy guidance, explainable assessment rules, accessible development and explicit boundaries around acceptable use so the duty to understand does not become a hidden workload
constraints: Where AI is embedded in infrastructure individuals do not choose, refusal shifts from individual use to procurement, policy, audit and contestability
target_learning_goals: AI literacy including the capacity to decide when a system should not be used and to justify one's relation to AI
examples: A researcher using AI-enabled search must understand enough to assess reliability, bias and attribution; a teacher educator preparing graduates for AI-mediated schools cannot simply refuse to understand AI
key_sources: Zagami, J. (2026). AI refusal in higher education: the right to refuse, the duty to understand and the diagnostic value of non-use. Higher Education Research & Development, 45(7), 2287-2294. https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2026.2694409

article_title: Teaching and Learning in the Social Context: A Meta-Analysis of Service Learning's Effects on Academic, Personal, Social, and Citizenship Outcomes
citation: Ruíz Montero, P. J., & Bru Serrano, M. (2021). La educación física y el deporte como servicio hacia los más vulnerables: beneficios del aprendizaje-servicio. Red Euroamericana de Investigación y Docencia en Educación Física. https://www.riadis.es
title: Red RIADIS de investigación en ApS en actividad física y deporte para la inclusión social
description: RIADIS es una red de investigación creada en 2019 por el Consejo Superior de Deportes que promueve el ApS universitario para integrar la actividad física y el deporte en colectivos vulnerables. Su investigación se centra en cinco colectivos: "(1) Infancia y adolescencia en situación de exclusión social; (2) Personas mayores vulnerables; (3) Personas con diversidad funcional y/o enfermedades crónicas; (4) Personas privadas de libertad; (5) Mujeres en situación de desventaja". Sus propósitos se concretan en cuatro grupos de acciones: dinamización, formación, investigación e innovación, y transferencia.
requirements: Conexión entre grupos de investigación y otras redes vinculadas al desarrollo humano y la educación para la justicia social
constraints: Creada y dinamizada mediante convocatorias del Consejo Superior de Deportes (2019 y 2020)
target_learners: profesionales de la actividad física y el deporte
colectivos en situación de vulnerabilidad socioeconómica
target_learning_goals: inclusión social mediante actividad física y deporte
examples: El catálogo es presentado como respuesta al compromiso de RIADIS con la transferencia social
key_sources: Ruíz Montero, P. J., & Bru Serrano, M. (2021). La educación física y el deporte como servicio hacia los más vulnerables: beneficios del aprendizaje-servicio. Red Euroamericana de Investigación y Docencia en Educación Física. https://www.riadis.es

article_title: Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens
citation: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522
title: The River conceptual model learning object
description: The River conceptual model is a Flash-based learning object designed for handheld use in geography fieldwork. It contains information about river parameters, enables calculation of river discharge, presents the impact of riverbed shape on flow rates, and allows identification of common bedrocks along the river. Students manipulate parameters such as position on the river via sliders, with outcomes displayed visually and numerically, and it can be rescaled for computers, projectors, and embedding in PowerPoint or blogs.
requirements: Designed for effective presentation in a 320x240 pixel screen area
Interaction via sliders and clickable spots supported across different devices
constraints: Zooming has not been utilized; a redesigned version should contain this facility, and semi-transparent panels are planned
target_learning_goals: understanding river parameters, discharge calculation, and downstream changes
examples: The screen was divided into functional areas: the top part presented the river cross-section and its changes, the bottom part presented related content and interactive elements
key_sources: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522

article_title: Improving the quality of vocational students’ collaboration and knowledge acquisition through instruction and joint reflection
citation: Elise H. Eshuis, Judith ter Vrugte, Anjo Anjewierden, Lars Bollen, Jakob Sikken, Ton de Jong. (2019). Improving the quality of vocational students' collaboration and knowledge acquisition through instruction and joint reflection. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2019) 14:53–76. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09296-0
title: RIDE rules for effective collaboration
description: The RIDE rules — Respect, Intelligent collaboration, Deciding together, and Encouraging — are communication rules summarizing essential characteristics of effective collaboration, derived by Saab et al. (2007) from a literature review and adapted for this study's vocational target group. The article states they "reflect communicative activities that are seen as essential for effective collaboration" and formed the basis for the definition of effective collaboration, driving both the classroom instruction's content and the reflection tool's assessment items and sub-rules (e.g., share relevant information, check if everyone agrees before acting, encourage others to participate).
requirements: Students need to know the RIDE rules; the instruction explains each rule's relevance with good and poor examples before collaboration begins.
constraints: The rules were originally tested as support for synchronous distance communication by Saab et al. (2007), not face-to-face vocational classrooms.
target_learning_goals: Collaboration skills and effective communication during collaborative inquiry learning
examples: Chat excerpts showing good and poor examples of each sub-rule were evaluated during instruction, and sub-rules were displayed in the tool's feed up and feed forward phases.
key_sources: Elise H. Eshuis, Judith ter Vrugte, Anjo Anjewierden, Lars Bollen, Jakob Sikken, Ton de Jong. (2019). Improving the quality of vocational students' collaboration and knowledge acquisition through instruction and joint reflection. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2019) 14:53–76. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09296-0

article_title: Highlighting tools and technologies for collaborative learning
citation: Carolyn P. Rosé, Nancy Law, Ulrike Cress, Sten Ludvigsen. (2019). Highlighting tools and technologies for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. (2019) 14:1–6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09297-z
title: Collaboration reflection tool with phase-differentiated Feed Up, Feed Back, and Feed Forward prompts
description: The joint reflection tool featured in the Eshuis et al. article prompted joint reflection during collaboration, with a focus on self- and peer-assessment as well as goal setting, in order to highlight the RIDE rules (Respect, Intelligent collaboration, Deciding together, and Encouraging). "Differential support was offered depending upon the phase, where the phases included Feed Up, Feed Back, and Feed Forward," and the interface presented questions with supporting information accessible through button clicks.
requirements: Used alongside collaborative activity so reflection occurs during collaboration, not only through pre-instruction
constraints: Support offered differentially by phase: Feed Up, Feed Back, and Feed Forward
target_learning_goals: collaborative skills including respect, intelligent collaboration, deciding together, and encouraging
examples: Students received instruction plus tool-mediated joint reflection, instruction alone, or neither, across three contrasted conditions
key_sources: Carolyn P. Rosé, Nancy Law, Ulrike Cress, Sten Ludvigsen. (2019). Highlighting tools and technologies for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. (2019) 14:1–6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09297-z

article_title: Supporting Communication in a Collaborative Discovery Learning Environment: the Effect of Instruction
citation: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W. R. & van Hout-Wolters, B. H. A. M. (2007). Supporting Communication in a Collaborative Discovery Learning Environment: the Effect of Instruction. Instructional Science 35:73–98. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-006-9003-4
title: RIDE rules: four principles for effective collaborative communication
description: The RIDE framework groups literature-derived characteristics of effective collaboration under four principles: Respect, Intelligent collaboration, Deciding together, and Encouraging. The article states that "The rules we extracted were grouped under four principles" and each rule carries sub-rules, such as 'everyone will have a chance to talk' for Respect and 'ask until you understand' for Encouraging. Each rule is mapped onto expected communicative activities, e.g. Intelligent collaboration onto informative responses, asking for understanding, and argumentative activities.
requirements: Instruction must be given before interaction and reminded during it, e.g. via prompts when assignments are opened
constraints: The Respect rule is represented by components not expressed in frequency of activities, so it was not analyzed via activity frequencies
target_learners: secondary school students aged 15–17 in pre-university physics education
target_learning_goals: effective collaborative communication during discovery learning in physics
examples: In the study, the rules were taught via a recorded computerized presentation with audio and visual explanation, example chats judged good or bad, and practice in a SimQuest application with prompts
key_sources: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W. R. & van Hout-Wolters, B. H. A. M. (2007). Supporting Communication in a Collaborative Discovery Learning Environment: the Effect of Instruction. Instructional Science 35:73–98. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-006-9003-4

article_title: Supporting Communication in a Collaborative Discovery Learning Environment: the Effect of Instruction
citation: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W. R. & van Hout-Wolters, B. H. A. M. (2007). Supporting Communication in a Collaborative Discovery Learning Environment: the Effect of Instruction. Instructional Science 35:73–98. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-006-9003-4
title: RIDE instructional program with prompts in a shared simulation discovery environment
description: A computerized instructional program that teaches the RIDE collaboration rules before learners work in a shared discovery learning environment, plus pop-up prompts reminding learners of the rules during tasks. The program "consisted of a recorded computerized presentation, where the rules were explained by both audio and visual means", followed by practice with example chats and a SimQuest logical-reasoning application, and an evaluation form. In the experimental version of Collisions, a prompt pops up whenever an assignment is opened, reminding learners of one of the RIDE rules; the control group received no pop-ups. Evaluation forms showed 83% of learners mentioned they applied the rules with ease.
requirements: Learners work in dyads on separate computers with a shared interface, communicating through a chat channel, in a simulation-based discovery learning environment
constraints: Reading prompts takes time, which the authors note can result in finishing fewer assignments in a fixed amount of time
target_learning_goals: effective communication and collaboration during collaborative discovery learning in physics
examples: Learners practiced the rules in a SimQuest application with RIDE-rule assignments and logical reasoning problems, then filled in an evaluation form together on screen
key_sources: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W. R. & van Hout-Wolters, B. H. A. M. (2007). Supporting Communication in a Collaborative Discovery Learning Environment: the Effect of Instruction. Instructional Science 35:73–98. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-006-9003-4

article_title: Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation
citation: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W., & van Hout-Wolters, B. (2012). Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 7-23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9068-6
title: RIDE rules: computerized instruction in effective collaboration communication
description: The RIDE instruction is a set of collaboration rules based on literature on effective collaboration, clustered under four principles: Respect, Intelligent collaboration, Deciding together, and Encouragement. It was delivered as "an introductory computerized instruction in the RIDE rules with which they could practice using the rules during collaboration", designed according to cognitive apprenticeship principles including modelling, coaching, scaffolding, articulation, and reflection.
requirements: Delivered in a session prior to collaborative work, with practice using the rules in dyads in a SimQuest simulation environment
constraints: In the first study, learners instructed in the RIDE rules used more communicative activities associated especially with the rules Deciding together and Encouraging
target_learners: secondary school students working in dyads in collaborative inquiry learning
target_learning_goals: effective communication and collaboration during inquiry learning
examples: Students in the experimental groups received the RIDE instruction before working 90 minutes with Collisions, and were prompted during the experiment to use the rules
key_sources: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W., & van Hout-Wolters, B. (2012). Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 7-23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9068-6

article_title: How Strong Is the Evidence for a Causal Reciprocal Effect? Contrasting Traditional and New Methods to Investigate the Reciprocal Effects Model of Self-Concept and Achievement
citation: Hübner, N., Wagner, W., Zitzmann, S., & Nagengast, B. (2023). How Strong Is the Evidence for a Causal Reciprocal Effect? Contrasting Traditional and New Methods to Investigate the Reciprocal Effects Model of Self-Concept and Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09724-6
title: RI-CLPM separates within-person processes from time-stable between-person differences, relaxing strong ignorability for time-invariant confounders
description: The random intercept cross-lagged panel model, introduced by Hamaker et al. (2015), adds random intercepts to the CLPM from a multilevel perspective in which repeated observations are nested within individuals. Its advantage is that "it separates processes that take place within individuals from time-stable observed and unobserved differences between individuals". The article notes the RI-CLPM requires strong ignorability and positivity to hold only after controlling for time-invariant differences between individuals, but cites simulation work questioning whether it controls unobserved confounding.
requirements: Covariates must be assessed prior to the repeated measures when RI-CLPMs are specified with covariates.
constraints: The article reports simulation evidence that RI-CLPMs are not necessarily able to control for unobserved confounding and yield biased estimates if the true model includes lag-2 effects.
target_learning_goals: estimating within-person reciprocal effects of self-concept and achievement
key_sources: Hübner, N., Wagner, W., Zitzmann, S., & Nagengast, B. (2023). How Strong Is the Evidence for a Causal Reciprocal Effect? article_title: Directional Ordering of Self-Concept, School Grades, and Standardized Tests Over Five Years: New Tripartite Models Juxtaposing Within- and Between-Person Perspectives
citation: Herbert W. Marsh, Reinhard Pekrun, & Oliver Lüdtke. (2022). Directional Ordering of Self-Concept, School Grades, and Standardized Tests Over Five Years: New Tripartite Models Juxtaposing Within- and Between-Person Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09662-9
title: Within-person (RI-CLPM) versus between-person (CLPM) perspectives on longitudinal panel data
description: A methodological framework distinguishing two ways of analyzing cross-lagged panel data. RI-CLPMs add stable trait factors and evaluate how "within-person deviations in one construct are related to subsequent within-person deviations in another construct," whereas "CLPMs confound the within- and between-person processes." The article argues the two models address different research questions, produce different interpretations, and should be juxtaposed rather than one treated as the default, with model choice resting on theoretical grounds as well as fit.
requirements: At least three waves of data for basic RI-CLPMs
Understanding that RI-CLPMs are person-centered/residualized statistical models, not tests of within-person mechanisms
constraints: Neither model provides good controls for unmeasured time-varying covariates
RI-CLPMs sometimes fail to converge to proper solutions even when the RI-CLPM structure generated the data
target_learning_goals: longitudinal analysis of self-concept and achievement relations
examples: The study operationalizes both models on the same PALMA dataset and compares their cross-lagged results

citation: Buckley, J., Sorby, S., Duffy, G., Maresch, G., & Power, J. (2026). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10149-0
title: RaumIntelligenzFörderung (RIF) platform for spatial ability development and measurement
description: The RIF platform (www.rif4you.eu) is an online spatial ability tool that "contains 1,600 spatial problems developed by experts in spatial ability and geometry organised into task groups which typically contain 20–60 problems". Task groups span nine spatial factors, with four higher-difficulty factors aimed at adolescents including mental rotation and spatial visualisation. Teachers assign task groups to class groups; performance is recorded as percentages of correct responses. In this study RIF served as both a development tool and a measurement instrument for Austrian adolescent data.
requirements: Use requires a teacher to set up a class group and assign task groups to students
constraints: The article states data from the RIF platform "has not been analysed to date with respect to its construct validity", so RIF-based inferences in the study are exploratory
target_learning_goals: Development of spatial ability across nine spatial factors including mental rotation and visualisation
examples: Austrian adolescent performance data on the spatial visualisation and mental rotation task groups were downloaded from the platform and analysed in this study

article_title: Recurrent individual treatment assignment: a treatment policy approach to account for heterogeneous treatment effects
citation: Ilja Cornelisz and Chris van Klaveren. (2022). Recurrent individual treatment assignment: a treatment policy approach to account for heterogeneous treatment effects. npj Science of Learning 7:3. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00117-4
title: Recurrent Individual Treatment Assignment (RITA) algorithm: sequential RCTs with rank-based probability updating that avoids explicit ITE estimation
description: RITA is a longitudinal individual assignment algorithm based on sequential RCTs or A/B-tests. Rather than estimating ITEs, it ranks each individual's observed treatment response each period, updates individual mean ranks per intervention, and adjusts assignment probabilities using an exponential learning parameter. The article states RITA 'refrains from attempting to estimate ITE and focuses on individual treatment response and assignment instead.' It maintains a minimum exploration level to allow for dynamic treatment effects.
requirements: Sequential RCT or A/B-test setting with recurrent assignment decisions over multiple periods
Observed treatment response variation across periods for each individual
Pre-specified upper and lower exploration bounds on assignment probabilities
constraints: Maintaining exploration leads to sub-optimal performance if no dynamic treatment effects exist
Performance depends on hyperparameter settings (learning parameter form, Bayesian updating modeling, number of interaction terms allowed)
Asymptotic properties, convergence, and optimality remain uninvestigated
target_learners: individuals in high-iterative educational or clinical settings
students in online adaptive practicing environments
target_learning_goals: optimizing which intervention, feedback, or adaptive practicing algorithm is assigned to each individual learner over time
examples: In the simulation study, RITA was applied to 1000 individuals across 60 periods with assignment probabilities initialized at 0.5 and exploration bounds set at 0.05/0.95
key_sources: Ilja Cornelisz and Chris van Klaveren. (2022). Recurrent individual treatment assignment: a treatment policy approach to account for heterogeneous treatment effects. npj Science of Learning 7:3. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00117-4

article_title: Recurrent individual treatment assignment: a treatment policy approach to account for heterogeneous treatment effects
citation: Ilja Cornelisz and Chris van Klaveren. (2022). Recurrent individual treatment assignment: a treatment policy approach to account for heterogeneous treatment effects. npj Science of Learning 7:3. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00117-4
title: Use RITA in high-iterative educational and clinical settings to account for unobserved heterogeneous treatment effects
description: The article recommends implementing RITA in settings where treatment decisions recur frequently and treatment response is observed each period, such as online adaptive practicing environments. It states 'Online or digital educational environments, for example, lend themselves exceptionally well for addressing heterogeneity with a RITA algorithm.' Practicing environments and feedback/nudge assignment are named applications.
requirements: High-iterative setting with recurrent assignment decisions and observable treatment response each period
Digital or online environment where the assigned intervention is not necessarily visible to the student
Willingness to accept probabilistic rather than deterministic assignment
constraints: Oscillating behavior may be problematic if switching costs are high (e.g., assigning students back and forth between very different learning methods)
A caliper can be built in to mitigate undesirable oscillating behavior
target_learners: students in online adaptive practicing environments
patients in clinical settings with monthly treatment updates
target_learning_goals: optimizing individual treatment assignment to improve intervention response
identifying which adaptive rule or feedback type works best for whom
examples: The article names practicing environments such as adaptive practicing programs and clinical medication assignment as implementation contexts

article_title: Looking Ahead to Select Tutorial Actions: A Decision-Theoretic Approach
citation: R. Charles Murray, Kurt Vanlehn, Jack Mostow. (2004). Looking Ahead to Select Tutorial Actions: A Decision-Theoretic Approach. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197308
title: Rich tutorial state model with knowledge, attention, affect, next actions, task progress and discourse state
description: The article's applications employ a tutorial state model that includes "the student's knowledge, focus of attention, affective state, and next action(s), along with task progress and the discourse state". This rich state model supplies the attributes over which the decision-theoretic action selection engines reason when looking ahead to the effects of candidate actions.
requirements: Attributes for student knowledge, attention, affect, next actions, task progress and discourse state must be modeled
examples: Employed by the calculus and elementary reading prototype engines described in the article

article_title: Impact of an instructional guide and examples on the quality of feedback: insights from a randomised controlled study
citation: George Gyamfi, Barbara E. Hanna, Hassan Khosravi. (2024). Impact of an instructional guide and examples on the quality of feedback: insights from a randomised controlled study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10346-0
title: RiPPLE learnersourcing platform with embedded feedback guide
description: RiPPLE is a teaching and research platform developed at the University of Queensland in which students create learning resources (multiple-choice questions, multi-answer questions, worked examples, and open-ended "notes") and moderate peers' resources before release to a shared bank. In this study the platform housed the intervention: "The guide, housed on RiPPLE, popped up the first time students began to provide feedback" and remained accessible thereafter. It also supports large-scale experimental research designs such as RCTs.
requirements: Students create and peer-moderate learning resources; a resource must be evaluated at least 3 times with an average of at least 3.5/5 to pass moderation
constraints: The study's guide was customisable to course contexts; the article notes limited understanding of the extent to which students re-consulted the guide after it first popped up
examples: 195 postgraduate applied linguistics students produced weekly reflection notes and completed 7231 moderations over 13 weeks

article_title: Relational topologies in the learning activity spaces: operationalising a sociomaterial approach
citation: Linda Castañeda, Victoria I. Marín, Daniel Villar-Onrubia. (2024). Relational topologies in the learning activity spaces: operationalising a sociomaterial approach. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10296-z
title: RICT case study: pre-service teacher-training course as testbed for the topologies
description: The RICT case is an on-campus pre-service teacher-training course, "Educational Resources and ICT for Primary School", at a Spanish university, taught in English to first-year students over 12 weeks (5 h per week) with 6 ECTS credits and an estimated workload of 150 h. The cohort included 50 students organised into eight stable working groups. The course is designed around a formal cooperative learning model with cooperative base groups, weekly trialogical learning tasks, and pre-established scripted roles. Data were collected in the academic year 2021-2022, starting at week 6, over 2 weeks, anonymously.
requirements: Group discussions, brainstorming dynamics, and online questionnaires for tool, space and device reporting
constraints: No identification or personal data were collected; supporting data is unavailable because participants did not agree to public sharing
examples: Students discussed tools in three categories (compulsory, discovered during tasks, pre-existing) and voted on the spaces they used most often

title: RiPPLE learning platform
description: RiPPLE is a discipline-agnostic learning platform operating at the course level, utilised to facilitate a student-centred, interactive, and collaborative learning environment. The platform incorporates learnersourcing, learning analytics, and adaptive learning mechanisms. Students generate learning resources (MCQs, worked examples, flashcards, slides, notes) and review peers' resources, which upon approval become accessible to the entire class for educational purposes.

article_title: The relationship of non-cognitive factors to academic and clinical performance in graduate rehabilitation science students in the United States: a systematic review.
citation: Reynolds K, Bazemore C, Hanebuth C, Hendren S, Horn M. (2021). The relationship of non-cognitive factors to academic and clinical performance in graduate rehabilitation science students in the United States: a systematic review. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2021.18.31
title: Richardson et al.'s framework of 5 non-intellective constructs
description: The review adopts a comprehensive framework from Richardson et al. to narrow the overly broad term non-cognitive, which has been used to include any factor outside GPA and standardized test scores. The framework describes "5 non-intellective constructs": "personality traits, motivational factors, self-regulatory learning strategies, students’ approaches to learning, and psychosocial contextual factors." These dimensions guided the review's eligibility criteria for which non-cognitive assessments qualified for inclusion.
requirements: Used to define inclusion criteria: studies must assess factors within these 5 domains
constraints: The review excludes variables rooted in cognition such as critical thinking and metacognition
target_learners: graduate rehabilitation science students (PT, OT, SLP)
target_learning_goals: organizing the study of non-cognitive factors related to academic and clinical performance
examples: The review used the framework's 5 dimensions to set selection criteria for included studies.

The relationship of non-cognitive factors to academic and clinical performance in graduate rehabilitation science students in the United States: a systematic review. article_title: Research education and training for nurses and allied health professionals: a systematic scoping review.
citation: King, O., West, E., Lee, S., Glenister, K., Quilliam, C., Wong, S. A., & Beks, H. (2022). Research education and training for nurses and allied health professionals: a systematic scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03406-7
title: Evaluate research education programs rigorously and include longer-term, organisation-level outcomes, not only individual-level measures
description: The review concludes that evaluation of research education programs must be rigorous and, although programs target individuals, evaluation must extend to longer-term and broader organisation-level outcomes and impacts. The authors argue that "Examining this is critical to improving clinician-led health research and the translation of research into clinical practice". This principle responds directly to the review's finding that few programs measured organisational or practice outcomes and that evaluation methods were poorly described.
requirements: Evaluation must consider longer-term and broader organisation-level outcomes and impacts, not only individual satisfaction, knowledge and confidence
constraints: Discerning education interventions from other elements of multidimensional RCB strategies is a fraught endeavour, complicating attribution of organisation-level impacts
target_learners: program evaluators and health organisation leaders
target_learning_goals: translation of research into clinical practice
examples: The review mapped 68 programs' outcomes to the modified Kirkpatrick typology and found few evaluated with research milestones such as protocol completion, manuscript preparation, poster or conference presentation

article_title: The Role of Cognate English-Kurdish Words in Teaching English
citation: Kasap, S. (2018). The role of cognate English–Kurdish words in teaching English. African Educational Research Journal, 6(4): 213-217. https://doi.org/10.30918/AERJ.64.18.046
title: Ringbom's three levels of cross-linguistic similarity transfer (general, item, and system level)
description: The article presents Ringbom's (2001) account of how similarity between languages supports transfer at "general level, item level and system level". The general level is students' overall perception of similarities between languages, encompassing shared alphabet and sound units up to grammatical structures and cognate structures. The article uses this framework to argue that awareness of cognates facilitates learning and understanding processes, and frames its own intervention as activating item-level orthographic similarity between Kurdish and English.
requirements: Learners must become aware of the similarities between the two languages' items and systems for the benefit to accrue
constraints: The article applies the framework to cognate (lexical) similarity between two Indo-European-related languages
target_learners: bilingual high-school students learning English as a foreign language
examples: The study group was instructed about Kurdish-English cognate structures such as Run–revan and Warm–Germ before the delayed post-test
key_sources: Kasap, S. (2018). The role of cognate English–Kurdish words in teaching English. African Educational Research Journal, 6(4): 213-217. https://doi.org/10.30918/AERJ.64.18.046

article_title: Digital Literacy and New Technological Perspectives
citation: Elvia Ilaria Feola. (2016). Digital Literacy and New Technological Perspectives. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(9): 2174-2180. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.040929
title: R-I-Z-A model for evaluating digital competence
description: The R-I-Z-A model structures competence assessment into four components: "(R) resources: understood as the knowledge and basic skills of the student; (I) interpretation: as the student defines situations; (Z) action: as the student acts in response to a problem; (A) self -regulation: as the student based on the experiences change their strategies according to the stresses from the environment". Following Trinchero, the four components of competence are held to emerge only when the subject faces problems. In the study, outgoing competence profiles were built with observable descriptors, declined in three levels (sufficient, good, very good), and assessment rubrics were administered every five weeks.
requirements: Competence descriptors must be observable and detectable; components emerge only when the subject is facing problems.
constraints: Output profiles were declined in only three evaluation levels: sufficient, good, very good.
target_learners: university students in primary education sciences
examples: Assessment rubrics were given every five meetings and afterwards used by students as a self-assessment tool.
key_sources: Elvia Ilaria Feola. (2016). Digital Literacy and New Technological Perspectives. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(9): 2174-2180. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.040929

article_title: Does motivation lead to academic success, or conversely? Reciprocal relations between autonomous and controlled motivation, and mathematics achievement.
citation: Santana‐Monagas, E., Núñez‐Regueiro, F., & Núñez, J. L. (2025). Does motivation lead to academic success, or conversely? Reciprocal relations between autonomous and controlled motivation, and mathematics achievement. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 513–529. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12736
title: RI-CLPM: separating within-person state changes from between-person trait differences in reciprocal-effects modelling
description: The random intercept cross-lagged panel model is a longitudinal modelling framework that adds random intercepts representing each student's own baseline level of motivation and achievement, treated as stable trait factors. The article states that "the RI‐CLPM separates within‐ and between‐person processes of change by adding random intercepts, which represent baseline levels in motivation and achievement estimated across the entire observation period". Remaining variance is interpreted as momentary within-person state changes modelled with autoregressive and cross-lagged effects, which the authors argue yields more reliable reciprocal-effect estimates than the classic CLPM, which confounds the two sources of change.
requirements: Three or more measurement waves of the dynamic constructs, with measurement invariance across time points
constraints: Causal processes identified are limited to the student level and do not inform on causalities at the class level; the article uses causality in the Granger-causal sense, which cannot establish ontological causality
target_learning_goals: Reciprocal longitudinal relations between academic motivation and mathematics achievement
examples: The study fit RI-CLPMs to three trimester waves of motivation self-reports and official school grades from 1042 students in 58 classes, with covariates (age, gender, track, school level) in Model 2
key_sources: Santana‐Monagas, E., Núñez‐Regueiro, F., & Núñez, J. L. (2025). Does motivation lead to academic success, or conversely? Reciprocal relations between autonomous and controlled motivation, and mathematics achievement. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 513–529. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12736

article_title: Academic motivation-achievement cycle and the behavioural pathways: A short-timeframe experiment with manipulated perceived achievement.
citation: Vu, T., Meeter, M., Hofman, A., Jansen, B., Magis‐Weinberg, L., van Triest, E., & van Atteveldt, N. (2025). Academic motivation–achievement cycle and the behavioural pathways: A short‐timeframe experiment with manipulated perceived achievement. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 683–722. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12731
title: Random-intercept cross-lagged panel modelling as a strategy for testing motivation–achievement reciprocity
description: The article applies the random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) to disentangle within-person temporal dynamics from stable between-person differences when testing whether motivation and achievement influence each other over time. The article explains that "the RI‐CLPM then separates stable between‐person differences (i.e., the invariant component) from within‐person fluctuations over time and the regression coefficients represent the amount of within‐person carry‐over." It uses bivariate and trivariate RI-CLPMs with likelihood-ratio and information-criteria model comparisons to test unilateral versus reciprocal links.
requirements: Multiple closely spaced measurement occasions (the study used eight time points within one hour) so within-person fluctuations can be modelled
A sample large enough for the targeted cross-lagged effect sizes; the authors' simulation targeted power above 0.75 at n = 300
constraints: The article argues the widely used CLPM is flawed by "the conflation of between‐ and within‐person variations", so findings from CLPM analyses are not directly comparable
Conclusions from non-experimental longitudinal designs remain limited to associations
examples: The study fit RI-CLPMs separately to the above-average and below-average rounds and compared cross-lagged and auto-regressive parameters across rounds

British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 683–722. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12731

article_title: The effect of a team-based blended simulation training program on cardiopulmonary resuscitation on healthcare professionals' perception, performance, and costs: a mixed-method study.
citation: Palmisano Francesco, Santuari Nadia, Moletta Cristina, Ambrosi Elisa, Rizzoli Andrea. (2024). The effect of a team-based blended simulation training program on cardiopulmonary resuscitation on healthcare professionals' perception, performance, and costs: a mixed-method study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06543-3
title: riAniMO blended team-based CPR/AED retraining program
description: riAniMO is a blended retraining program combining a 90-minute e-learning preparatory phase (video lessons, a virtual CPR resuscitation simulation with gamification, and an ad hoc device simulator) with a roughly 60-minute in situ team-based BLS/AED simulation in the participant's own clinical unit. Per the article, "The riAniMO is based on a multimedia training program with video lessons and a virtual CPR resuscitation simulation, and a team-based CPR and AED simulation." Three five-minute scenarios are run with two facilitators, followed by 15-minute debriefings, and performance is assessed with an 11-item checklist covering technical and non-technical skills.
requirements: Participants must have previously completed the ERC BLS/AED course
Facilitators require ERC BLSD instructor certification plus one day of debriefing training, 2 hours of expert observation, and 2 hours of supervised simulation practice
constraints: Developed for and evaluated within the APSS Trento hospital network; requires organizational effort and carries risk of last-minute cancellations due to workload or setting unavailability
target_learners: Healthcare professionals (nurses, physicians, technical and sociosanitary staff) undergoing biennial BLSD recertification
target_learning_goals: Maintenance of CPR and AED technical skills
Non-technical skills such as teamwork, leadership, and communication
examples: In 2022 the program retrained 1,167 HCPs across two city hospitals and five community hospitals using Resusci Anne QCPR simulators connected to the units' own defibrillators
key_sources: Palmisano Francesco, Santuari Nadia, Moletta Cristina, Ambrosi Elisa, Rizzoli Andrea. (2024). The effect of a team-based blended simulation training program on cardiopulmonary resuscitation on healthcare professionals' perception, performance, and costs: a mixed-method study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06543-3

article_title: The effect of a team-based blended simulation training program on cardiopulmonary resuscitation on healthcare professionals' perception, performance, and costs: a mixed-method study.
citation: Palmisano Francesco, Santuari Nadia, Moletta Cristina, Ambrosi Elisa, Rizzoli Andrea. (2024). The effect of a team-based blended simulation training program on cardiopulmonary resuscitation on healthcare professionals' perception, performance, and costs: a mixed-method study. title: riAniMO pedagogical framework mapping learning theories to training phases
description: The article explicitly grounds the riAniMO program in a set of pedagogical theories assigned to its two phases: individual constructivism and experiential learning for the e-learning preparatory phase, and social constructivism, experiential learning, and situated learning for the in-situ simulation phase. As printed, "The RiAniMO project is based on various pedagogical theories as shown in Table 1." The e-learning phase lets individuals experiment in an online environment with gamified reviews and on-demand paths, while the simulation phase uses horizontal peer and facilitator feedback, progressive scenarios, and reflection on experience in the real workplace.
requirements: Both an online e-learning environment and access to real clinical settings with the unit's own devices are needed to enact the two-phase design
constraints: The mapping is the authors' design rationale, not an empirically tested comparison of theoretical components
target_learners: Healthcare professionals in hospital and community settings
target_learning_goals: Teamwork and reflection on emergency management
examples: Table 1 assigns experiential learning to both phases, with game mechanics such as prizes, points, and challenges online and pause-and-rest reflection moments during simulation

article_title: RiNeo MR: A mixed reality simulator for newborn life support training.
citation: Coduri Mara, Calandrino Andrea, Addiego Mobilio Giulia, Casadio Maura, Ricci Serena. (2023). RiNeo MR: A mixed reality simulator for newborn life support training. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0294914
title: RiNeo MR: a mixed-reality newborn life support training simulator combining a sensorized manikin with a VR application
description: RiNeo MR combines a sensorized newborn manikin and face mask with a Unity3D VR application of delivery and operating room scenarios, communicating in real time. It monitors four tasks: "head positioning, mask positioning, positive pressure ventilation, and chest compression". It offers a 2D screen-based mode with real-time feedback and a 3D immersive mode where virtual and real manikins are overlapped, providing passive haptics.

Hand tracking can be lost when hands cross virtual objects, and the trackers used are cumbersome

target_learning_goals: newborn life support resuscitation skills: head positioning, mask positioning, positive pressure ventilation, chest compression
examples: 16 subjects performed resuscitation manoeuvres in both 2D and 3D modes and completed UEQ, SUS, SSQ and IPQ questionnaires

article_title: Validation and Adaptation of the Academic-Resilience Scale in the Spanish Context.
citation: Trigueros Rubén, Magaz-González Ana M., García-Tascón Marta, Alias Antonio, Aguilar-Parra José M. (2020). Validation and Adaptation of the Academic-Resilience Scale in the Spanish Context. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17113779
title: Richardson's metatheory of resilience as the organizing account of academic resilience, and its stated limitations
description: The article frames academic resilience within Richardson's metatheory of resilience, which explains the mechanisms people use "to try to overcome and adapt to the possible vicissitudes they face". Resilience begins in physical, mental and spiritual balance; adversity disrupts this homeostasis when resources are insufficient, and the individual readjusts and returns to balance by raising their level of resilience, or else homeostasis and resilience decrease. The article also reports the metatheory's noted limits: it treats resilience linearly and neglects how emotions affect adaptation.
requirements: A situation of physical, mental, and spiritual balance that is disrupted by an adverse situation the individual lacks resources or skills to cope with
constraints: Criticized as analyzing resilience from a linear point of view and not analyzing how emotions affect the process of adaptation
target_learning_goals: understanding how students adapt to and overcome academic difficulties
examples: the article cites studies showing anxiety, depression and stress contribute to the decrease of resilience due to continuous failure

title: Risk-adjusted CUSUM learning-curve method for evaluating intubation training
description: The cumulative summation (CUSUM) control-chart method is the study's primary outcome measure for charting each trainee's learning curve across intubation attempts. The article defines a risk-adjusted variant in which "the CUSUM at time t (ct) is ct = ct–1+ (xt–x0)", where xt is 1 for failure and 0 for success and x0 is the patient's estimated risk from logistic regression. It sets a 98% target first-attempt success rate and plots standard and risk-adjusted charts per trainee.
requirements: Setting an acceptable failure rate (p0 = 20%) and unacceptable failure rate (p1 = 40%), type I and II error rates (α, β = 0.1), and a target success rate based on senior doctors' experience; a risk score per patient from logistic regression on difficulty factors
constraints: The article states the standard CUSUM method "does not allow weighting of the CUSUM score based on the expected difficulty of each procedure", which motivated the risk-adjusted variant; there is no authoritative criterion for evaluating intubation learning performance
target_learners: Novice trainees learning endotracheal intubation in anesthesiology or emergency medicine
target_learning_goals: Objectively tracking procedural skill acquisition and determining the number of attempts needed to reach a target success rate
